title: The Queue ADT and the Linear-Queue Problem
quickIdea: A queue inserts at the rear and removes at the front, so the oldest item leaves first. On a plain array the freed slots at the front are never reused, and shifting to recover them costs O(n) per dequeue.
remember: Operations: enqueue at the rear, dequeue at the front, front/rear reads, isEmpty, isFull. All are O(1) on a circular array or a linked list.
Linear array implementation: front and rear only move forward. After k dequeues the first k slots are dead, and rear eventually reaches the end while the queue is short.
If a dequeue shifts the remaining elements left to keep them at index 0, dequeue costs Theta(n) and enqueue stays O(1). That is the naive implementation the 2016 question rules out.
The fix is to treat the array as circular, wrapping both indices modulo the array size, so every slot is reusable and both operations stay O(1).
A queue on a linked list keeps head and tail pointers, so enqueue at the tail and dequeue at the head are both O(1) with no capacity limit.

example.prompt: An array of size 5 holds a linear queue. Enqueue a, b, c; dequeue twice; then enqueue d and e. What happens?
example.work: After the three enqueues rear = 3 and front = 0. Two dequeues move front to 2 and free slots 0 and 1. Enqueue d writes at 3 and sets rear = 4; enqueue e would write at 4 and set rear = 5, which is past the end, so the queue reports full although only three elements are stored and slots 0 and 1 are empty.
example.answer: The fifth enqueue reports full with two slots free - the linear-queue defect.

gateAngle: The 2016 Set 1 question is the cost version of this card: it asks which implementation makes both operations O(1), and the answer is the circular array. Reading a queue implementation means asking where front and rear point and whether either wraps.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: A queue is implemented on an array of size 5 by shifting all remaining elements one slot left on every dequeue. Give the worst-case cost of enqueue and of dequeue, and the cost of n alternating operations.
variations.answer: Enqueue O(1), dequeue O(n); n alternating operations cost Theta(n^2).
variations.why: This is exactly the implementation the 2016 question rejects. Each dequeue moves up to n - 1 elements, so a sequence of n operations is quadratic - the reason the circular array exists.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: After enqueue a, b, c and one dequeue on a linear queue held in an array, where are front and rear, and how many elements are stored?
variations.answer: front = 1, rear = 3, two elements (b and c).
variations.why: front advances past the removed a and rear is the next free slot, so the live elements are at indices 1 and 2. The element count is rear - front = 2 in this convention, and slot 0 is already dead space.

trap.what: Assuming that a queue built on an array gives O(1) dequeue because it gives O(1) enqueue.
trap.why: Without wraparound, keeping the queue contiguous forces a shift on every dequeue. The asymmetry comes from the layout, not from the abstract data type: both operations are O(1) on a circular array or a linked list.
trap.counterexample: Dequeue the first of 1,000,000 queued items in a shifting implementation: 999,999 elements move. In a circular array the same dequeue moves front by one and copies nothing.

check.question: In a linear array queue with front = 1 and rear = 3 (rear is the next free slot), how many elements are stored?
check.explanation: The live slots are 1 and 2, so the count is rear - front = 3 - 1 = 2. Slot 0 is dead space left by the earlier dequeue.
